title: Steamed Sea Bass with Ginger
subtitle: Whole sea bass steamed with ginger and spring onion, finished with sizzling hot oil
excerpt: A whole sea bass is steamed over boiling water until just cooked, then covered with ginger, spring onion and soy sauce and doused with a ladleful of smoking hot oil that sizzles and cooks the garnish on contact. It is one of the fastest and most impressive dishes in Chinese home cooking. Serves 4 in about 25 minutes.
sourceNotes: Steaming whole fish and finishing with hot poured oil is a technique central to Cantonese seafood cookery and is discussed in detail in Eileen Yin-Fei Lo's 'The Chinese Kitchen' (William Morrow, 1999). The method is also covered in Yan-Kit So's 'Classic Food of China' (Macmillan, 1992), which notes that the quality of the soy sauce poured over the fish is as important as the freshness of the fish itself.

glossaryTerms.definition: A technique in which a small amount of oil is heated to smoking point in a ladle or pan and then poured directly over a garnish of ginger, spring onion or herbs arranged on the dish. The sizzling oil blooms the aromatics instantly and gives the dish a characteristic fragrance and slight caramelisation.

A Chinese fermented rice wine named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. It has a rich, slightly nutty flavour and is used in marinades and sauces throughout Chinese cooking. Dry sherry makes a reasonable substitute.

A thin, pale soy sauce with a clean, salty flavour used as a seasoning and table condiment. It is distinct from dark soy sauce, which is thicker, sweeter and used mainly for colour. For steamed fish, light soy sauce is essential as dark soy would overwhelm the delicate flavour.

Cooking fish over boiling water in a sealed environment so it cooks gently in its own steam. The technique preserves moisture and produces a silky texture that frying or baking cannot match. The fish is done when the flesh at the thickest point near the backbone flakes easily and is opaque throughout.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 25 minutes. The
time depends on the weight of the fish: allow roughly 8 minutes per 500g, but check early by pressing the flesh near the dorsal fin. It should give slightly and look opaque all the way through.

items.prepNote: half sliced, half cut into fine matchsticks
2 halved lengthways for steaming, 2 cut into fine strips

content.text: Score the fish two or three times on each side, cutting down to the bone. Rub inside and out with {{shaoxing-wine}} and season the cavity lightly with salt. Place the sliced ginger and halved spring onions in the cavity and under the fish on the steaming plate.

Bring water in a wok or large pot to a full boil. Set a steaming rack in the wok and lower the fish on its plate onto the rack. Cover with a tight-fitting lid and steam for 10 to 12 minutes for a 700g fish.
While the fish steams, prepare the garnish: pile the matchstick ginger and fine spring onion strips in a small bowl. Mix the {{light-soy-sauce}} with the {{sesame-oil}} in a separate bowl.

When the fish is just cooked, carefully lift it out of the steamer. Pour away any liquid that has pooled on the plate (it will be slightly bitter from the fish juices). Pour the soy and sesame oil mixture over the fish.

Scatter the matchstick ginger, spring onion strips and coriander leaves over the fish. Heat the {{vegetable-oil}} in a small pan over a high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Immediately pour it over the garnish. It will sizzle loudly and cook the aromatics on contact. Serve at once.

items.symptom: The fish is overcooked and dry
items.cause: It steamed for too long or the fish was too thin
items.fix: Check a minute or two early by pressing the flesh near the backbone. A smaller or thinner fish may be done in 8 minutes.

items.symptom: The liquid on the plate tastes bitter
items.cause: Fish juices have mixed with the steam condensate
items.fix: Always tip away the accumulated liquid before pouring on the soy sauce. This step is not optional.

items.symptom: The hot oil does not sizzle when poured
items.cause: The oil was not hot enough
items.fix: The oil must be smoking before it goes on. Heat it in the smallest pan you have over the highest heat and watch for the first wisps of smoke.

content.text: Cantonese steamed fish is the centrepiece of family meals across Hong Kong and Guangdong. It appears at celebratory dinners and on weeknight tables alike. The same technique applies to other white fish: sea bream, red snapper and tilapia all work well. The
rubbed into the cavity before steaming removes any residual fishiness and flavours the flesh from the inside.
